Abstract
Since the end of Dennard scaling, power consumption has become a primary con-
straint in computing hardware design because it no longer scales proportionally
with transistor size. The push for increased performance has led manufacturers
to develop multi-core devices, revolutionizing the field over the past few decades.
Recently, the High Performance Computing field has focused on energy-efficient
heterogeneous platforms, with Field-Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGAs) gaining
attention due to their superior energy efficiency. Traditionally, FPGAs were ex-
cluded from mainstream software development due to the complex design process,
but this is changing with the introduction of High-Level Synthesis (HLS) tools that
generate hardware descriptions from standard programming languages like C++.
Numerical Linear Algebra (NLA) traverses several disciplines of science and
engineering and is crucial in scientific computing. Solving problems in these ar-
eas often involves basic NLA operations, which are typically the most computa-
tionally expensive steps. This thesis focuses on developing and evaluating NLA
kernels using HLS tools on modern FPGA-based platforms. To support this, we
set up a laboratory for measuring the performance and energy consumption of
heterogeneous platforms.
This step involves the acquisition and installation of
FPGA-based acceleration platforms, along with the necessary development tools
and infrastructure. The thesis evaluates the performance of FPGAs for both dense
and sparse NLA operations using floating-point arithmetic, comparing the results
against multi-core CPUs.
The study begins with a review of the state-of-the-art in HLS implementations
on FPGA. It then explores developments in two of the most prominent dense linear
algebra kernels: matrix-vector multiplication (GEMV) and matrix-matrix multi-
plication (GEMM). Additionally, the thesis focuses on one of the key kernels in
sparse linear algebra, sparse matrix-vector multiplication (SpMV). The findings
indicate that while CPUs often outperform FPGAs in dense operations, FPGAs
offer competitive energy efficiency. For sparse operations, FPGAs not only de-
liver competitive performance but also consistently demonstrate superior energy
efficiency.
A key aspect of maximizing kernel efficiency is exploring analytical tools to
understand performance and guide the optimization process. The roofline model
(RLM) is a well-known graphical tool that facilitates the analysis of computational
performance and identifies primary bottlenecks. We propose a novel extension of
the RLM for FPGAs to assist in the optimization of runtime and energy con-


sumption for NLA kernels based on sparse blocked storage formats. We apply this
extended model to our SpMV kernel with a block-sparse storage format.
The final effort in this thesis focuses on the analysis and extension of AMD’s
Vitis library for the SpMV operation, recognized as state-of-the-art in the field.
Several optimizations and matrix preprocessing techniques were explored, leading
to significant performance gains. Among these extensions, techniques were intro-
duced that combine reducing block sizes (to minimize padding) with the concurrent
processing of multiple blocks (to compensate for the reduced data processed per
block). For single precision, the optimizations achieved an average speedup of 1.5×
and a maximum of 3.7×. Furthermore, a custom SpMV kernel optimized for band
matrices was developed, delivering substantial performance improvements over the
Vitis kernel for these kind of matrices.

Introduction
1.1
Hardware acceleration
What is the significance of hardware acceleration with FPGAs? Why do we invest
substantial effort in designing our algorithms to be more closely aligned with the
hardware? These questions are crucial for understanding the motivations behind
our work. To address them, we need to delve into the recent history of computing
platform design.
According to Moore’s Law [1], over the last decades, the number of tran-
sistors per integrated circuit has approximately doubled every two years. This
phenomenon, along with Dennard’s Scaling — which demonstrates how shrinking
transistors can increase their speed and energy efficiency — provided processor
manufacturers with a straightforward path to achieve remarkable performance
increases. By advancing to the next generation of transistor scaling, they could
increase the operating frequency and almost double the performance. These years,
spanning from the 1980s to the mid-2000s, were considered the golden age of se-
quential computing.
However, by 2006, Dennard Scaling [2] came to an end and the free lunch was
over [3]. Transistor scaling no longer enhanced energy efficiency, as leakage cur-
rents began to dominate, and the scaling of voltage and frequency in processors
reached a halt. The industry’s imperative to keep pace with Moore’s Law — which
had become something of a self-fulfilling prophecy — coupled with the demands
for increased performance, prompted manufacturers to shift toward multi-core de-
vices [4].
Since then, we have witnessed a remarkable revolution in multi-core
processors initially and, subsequently, in other heterogeneous platforms such as
Graphics Processing Unit (GPU). Nevertheless, with each generation of transistor
scaling, the challenge lies in powering all transistors within a chip [5] to extract
the best performance from all the cores. This scenario explains why power con-
sumption has become the primary concern in system design.
An alternative perspective emerges from High-Performance Computing (HPC)
centers, including data center and supercomputers, which have proliferated in
recent decades due to the data explosion and the demand for sophisticated com-

puting systems. These facilities are hungry consumers of energy, a reality that is
increasingly worrying the HPC community [6], given the constrained power and
cooling capabilities of HPC centers, and exacerbated by high electricity costs. Also,
although to a lesser extent, the environmental impact of energy consumption is
gaining visibility [7]. These concerns have led manufacturers and users in a quest
for energy-efficient platforms. In this context, the FPGA — recently rediscovered
as an interesting alternative to other heterogeneous devices — is gaining attention
in the HPC world due to its superior energy efficiency.
FPGAs play a crucial role in shaping architecture-specific solutions, provid-
ing not only minimal latency but also high-throughput implementations. Their
ability to create customized data paths, expose fine-grained parallelism, and min-
imize control logic overhead grants them remarkable flexibility and performance.
Consequently, these devices have found a niche in applications such as telecom-
munications equipment [8]. Nevertheless, certain challenges such as limited peak
floating-point performance and the requirement to use low-level Hardware Descrip-
tion Languages (HDL) like VHDL or Verilog — which demand specialized knowl-
edge of the underlying hardware — have kept FPGAs somewhat distanced from
the HPC community.
This scenario began to evolve in the last decade as FPGA manufacturers
started investing in high-end devices equipped with numerous dedicated hard-
ware multipliers and increased memory bandwidths. Moreover, substantial efforts
have been made to adopt High-Level Synthesis (HLS) tools, enabling the genera-
tion of hardware descriptions from high-level algorithms written in languages like
C/C++ or OpenCL. This shift may address the programming productivity needs
of the software HPC community, making FPGAs a viable alternative to other
many-core devices. A notable example of this investment trend is apparent in the
strategic maneuvers by semiconductor industry giants, as seen in Intel’s acquisition
of Altera in 2015 and AMD’s acquisition of Xilinx in 2022.
The emergence of FPGAs in the domain of HPC solutions, especially those
with a pronounced focus on energy efficiency, requires a comprehensive approach.
Manufacturers assume a crucial role in the development of efficient platforms char-
acterized by the focus on dedicated hardware (e.g. multipliers, high-bandwidth
memory) and HLS tools.
Simultaneously, there is a parallel need to develop
power-aware algorithms capable of effectively harnessing the capabilities of these
advanced platforms. This dual perspective implies not only optimizing algorithms
for enhanced performance but also strategically identifying the optimal combi-
nation of hardware platforms and algorithms to maximize overall efficiency and
benefits in the pursuit of energy-efficient HPC solutions. This approach serves as
a fundamental guiding principle for the research conducted in this thesis.
1.2
Numerical linear algebra
Numerical Linear Algebra (NLA) traverses several disciplines of science and engi-
neering, such as artificial intelligence, optimization, computer graphics and con-
trol, and is a field of great importance in scientific computing. Solving problems in

1.2. Numerical linear algebra
these areas often includes, as the most computationally expensive step, basic NLA
operations such as the general matrix-matrix multiplication (GEMM), general
matrix-vector multiplication (GEMV) or the operation of multiplying a sparse
matrix by a vector (SpMV) [9,10].
In deep learning, the most computationally intensive layers are the convolu-
tional and fully connected layers [11]. The former can be represented as a GEMM
operation, while the latter can be implemented using either GEMM or GEMV.
Furthermore, neural network training heavily depends on GEMM [12]. The back
propagation algorithm, a cornerstone of neural network training, requires repeated
application of GEMM to update the network weights. During the forward pass,
GEMM calculates the weighted sum of input features, and during the backward
pass, it efficiently computes the gradients with respect to the weights.
Graph analysis is fundamental in various domains, including social network
analysis and biological network modeling. SpMV plays a central role in algorithms
for graph traversal and analysis. The PageRank algorithm, used by search engines
to rank web pages [13], relies on iterative SpMV operations with the adjacency
matrix of the graph to compute importance scores. Another well known context for
the SpMV is the resolution of linear systems of equations by iterative methods.
This involves the repeated use of the SpMV operation, maintaining the same
sparse matrix but varying the vector to be multiplied. The importance of this
sparse NLA kernel in the community has motivated a significant amount of work
focused on its optimization and performance improvement [14,15].
Additionally, iterative methods are typically employed to solve large systems
of linear equations, such as those arising from finite element methods (FEM) for
Partial Differential Equations (PDE), structural analysis, and circuit simulations.
The Conjugate Gradient (CG) algorithm [16, 17], a prominent iterative solver,
heavily relies on matrix-vector multiplication operations. This is critical for solving
sparse systems from very large-scale problems (e.g., FEM). It should be noted
that direct methods require matrix factorization, which may be impractical due
to limited memory, as factored matrices can become dense.
Numerical Linear Algebra is a research field characterized by the utilization
of kernel libraries that have become de facto standards. A notable example is
the Basic Linear Algebra Subprograms (BLAS) specification for elementary dense
matrix operations. The development of NLA has followed a layered approach to
kernel specifications, shaping the landscape of dense operations since the 1970s.
This evolution began with the BLAS-1 specification [18], followed by BLAS-2 [19],
BLAS-3 [20], and later, the Linear Algebra Package (LAPACK) [21] and ScaLA-
PACK [22] libraries. These kernels are fundamental to many scientific programs
and often dominate execution time and energy consumption [23], prompting nu-
merous efforts to improve their performance and efficiency [24].
In the sparse
domain, this effort is reflected in the efficient implementation of kernels such as
SpMV, Sparse Triangular Solver (SpTRSV), and General Sparse Matrix-Matrix
Multiplication (SpGEMM). A good example is the Sparse BLAS standard, an
extension of the BLAS specification designed to efficiently handle unstructured
sparse matrices.

The importance of NLA is also supported by the strong presence of basic al-
gebra operations in the most widespread benchmarks. One of the most notable is
the LINPACK benchmark [25], which is employed to define the Top500 list [26],
ranking the 500 most powerful non-distributed computer systems in the world.
Linpack employs LU-factorization to assess the peak performance achievable by a
specific combination of hardware platform and software implementations. On the
other hand, in the sparse field there is Graph500 [27], a benchmark for supercom-
puters based on large-scale graph analysis. Another prominent example is the fact
that the SpMV kernel constitutes the core of the High Performance Conjugate
Gradients (HPCG) Benchmark [28]. HPCG serves as a complement to the High
Performance LINPACK (HPL) benchmark.
1.3
Objectives
In the context described above, the main purpose of this thesis is to explore FPGAs
as a platform for the efficient acceleration of NLA operations, focusing on execution
time and energy consumption. Our work is oriented towards HPC applications,
meaning that high-performance FPGAs are employed. These devices are geared
towards data center or scientific computing applications, with large computing and
memory bandwidth requirements.
The primary objective is to develop and evaluate NLA operations using HLS
tools on modern FPGA-based platforms. As part of this evaluation, it is essential
to compare the performance of NLA operations on other heterogeneous devices,
such as multi-core CPUs. Additionally, we aim to assess HLS tools to determine

Review of NLA operations
The purpose of this section is to provide a comprehensive overview of the NLA
operations utilized within this thesis, offering insights into their methodologies
and applications. This includes details of the specific mathematical operations
involved.
The BLAS (Basic Linear Algebra Subprograms) [29] has become one of the
most essential libraries for HPC due to its efficiency, portability and availabil-
ity. BLAS is composed of routines for computing common dense linear algebra
operations. It is organized into levels according to the degree of complexity (i.e.
the number of computations involved). The level 1 involves scalar, vector and
vector-vector operations, the level 2 includes matrix-vector operations, and the
level 3 performs matrix-matrix operations. BLAS libraries have become one of the
main building blocks in linear algebra applications, such as solving linear system
of equations, linear least square problems or eigenvalue problems.
In the field of sparse linear algebra, research efforts have primarily concen-
trated on the efficient implementation of a select set of kernels, including SpMV,
SpTRSV, and SpGEMM. Among these, SpMV stands out as a fundamental op-
eration due to its central role in scientific and engineering applications, such as
iterative solvers and graph analytics.
This motivated our decision to focus on
optimizing SpMV in this study.
In the following sections we describe the most relevant kernels from dense and
sparse NLA appearing in this work. Complementary, we present some of the most
relevant sparse matrix representation formats.

2.1.3
Sparse matrices
A matrix is considered sparse when the majority of its elements are zero. This mo-
tivates the use of storage structures that exploit this characteristic. Specifically,
only the non-zero coefficients are typically stored, along with indices that indi-
cate their positions in the matrix. Unlike dense matrices, where all elements are
stored and processed, sparse matrices utilize specialized storage formats — such as
Compressed Sparse Row (CSR), Compressed Sparse Column (CSC), or Coordi-
nate (COO) format — to efficiently manage non-zero elements and their indices.
This approach significantly reduces memory usage and computational overhead,
especially in large-scale systems. The sparsity of a matrix is defined as the ratio of
zero elements to the total number of elements. However, there is no universally ac-
cepted threshold for how many zero elements a matrix must have to be considered
sparse.
2.1.3.1
Banded matrices
A banded matrix is a matrix in which non-zero elements are concentrated around
the main diagonal, forming a diagonal band. For a square matrix A = (ai,j), the
band is defined by two constants:
• The lower bandwidth kl, which is the largest k such that ai,j = 0 for all
i > j + kl.
• The upper bandwidth ku, which is the largest k such that ai,j = 0 for all
j > i + ku.
Together, kl and ku define a band where all non-zero elements of the matrix are
contained.
The bandwidth (B) of the matrix is often defined as the maximum between
the lower and the upper bandwidths. That is, the number k > 0 such that ai,j = 0
if |i−j| > k. It can also be defined as the sum of the lower and upper bandwidths,
plus one for the main diagonal (B = kl + ku + 1). In this work, we adopt this
definition of bandwidth.

2.1.5
Sparse matrix-vector multiplication (SpMV)
The Sparse Matrix-Vector multiplication (SpMV) is essential in the sparse NLA
field as it is one of the most time-consuming stages in many applications. An exam-
ple is the solution of linear systems of equations using Krylov subspace methods.
These methods require the repeated use of the SpMV kernel, keeping the same ma-
trix and changing the dense vector. The importance of this kernel has motivated
numerous efforts targeting its optimization and performance improvement [14,15].
Accompanying this effort is the historical evolution of HPC platforms, which is why
there are efficient implementations of SpMV for the most widespread hardware
platforms.
The serial version of the SpMV is shown in Algorithm 1, where the sparse
matrix A is stored in CSR format [32]. The non-zero elements are stored in the
array values, the column index of each element in the matrix A is stored in an
array col ind, and row ptr stores the index of the first element for each row in
vector values. The non-zero elements within each row are arranged by column
index.
The main approach to parallelize this operation using the CSR format is to
exploit the absence of data dependencies between the computations associated with
each row. However, this method presents severe load imbalances — depending on
the sparsity pattern — and suffers from indirect data access to the dense vector x.

2.2.1
FPGA architecture
Unlike other heterogeneous platforms, such as GPUs, FPGAs do not have a
predefined high-level architecture.
Instead, they consist of a matrix of config-
urable logic blocks (i.e., logic elements) and integrated blocks with fixed func-
tions2, such as memories, Digital Signal Processing units (DSPs), clock man-
agers, and transceivers. The interconnection of these blocks is achieved through
a programmable routing structure.
FPGAs also include several programmable
input/output pins for interfacing with external devices, facilitating the implemen-
tation of multiple communication protocols. Figure 2.1 depicts a simplified struc-
ture of the FPGA, providing details on the programmable logic structure and a
simplified version of a logic element.
FPGAs are not programmed in the sense typically associated with software
development. Unlike conventional programming, where code is written to be ex-
ecuted by a processing unit, FPGA design involves describing a logic circuit’s
behavior using Hardware Description Languages (HDLs). This abstract descrip-
tion is transformed by the synthesis tool into a logic circuit based on the resources
of the FPGA. In the next step, the circuit architecture is mapped to specific logical

From a technological perspective, FPGAs occupy a middle ground between
Application-Specific Integrated Circuits (ASICs) and general-purpose processors.
Unlike ASICs, FPGAs offer significant flexibility as they can be reprogrammed
after the manufacturing process. They have shorter development times and avoid
the extremely high initial costs associated with ASICs. However, ASICs have the
advantage of being optimized for maximum efficiency and performance, and once
the manufacturing process is completed, their per-unit costs are much lower at
high volumes.
The configurable logic block (or logic element) is the smallest programmable
unit of the FPGA. In their simplest form, these blocks are composed of a pro-
grammable Look-Up Table (LUT), a register, and a programmable selector that
takes either the LUT’s output or the register’s output.
LUTs can implement
small logic functions, and their value is set during the FPGA programming stage.
Combining multiple (up to thousands or millions) LUTs and registers allows the
generation of complex logic functions or state machines.
The clock’s operating frequency of a given FPGA design depends on the syn-
thesized circuit, but it is usually lower than other heterogeneous devices. This
is a consequence of supporting reconfigurability.
FPGAs also offer lower peak
floating-point performance than GPUs and less memory bandwidth, but this may

of DSP blocks (that allow TFLOPS performance) and high memory bandwidth.
These characteristics, in combination with the HLS tools available, are making
these devices increasingly attractive in the HPC domain.
2.2.2
Hardware acceleration with FPGAs
As stated in Chapter 1, FPGAs have emerged as a versatile hardware acceler-
ation platform for various applications. These devices are highly customizable,
allowing for optimized data paths with very low latency, and providing significant
performance improvements in parallelizable tasks. Additionally, FPGAs can be
more energy-efficient than CPUs and GPUs for certain workloads, as they can be
tailored to perform specific tasks with minimal overhead. However, FPGA de-
velopment requires a deep understanding of hardware design and is much more
time-consuming than software development for CPUs or GPUs.
The typical setup for hardware acceleration with FPGAs consists of a CPU
acting as a host, coupled with one or more accelerators. The host offloads the most
compute-intensive tasks to the accelerators to speed up the algorithms. Commu-
nication between the host and FPGA device is typically facilitated by the PCI Ex-
press (PCIe) interface, which provides high-speed, low-latency data transfer. The
speed of PCIe depends on the version and configuration of the interface. Modern
PCIe Gen5 interfaces can provide bit rates of up to 32 GT/s (giga-transfers per
second) per lane, with typical configurations supporting 16 lanes, resulting in total
bandwidths of up to 64 GB/s.
The data transfer rates between the host and the accelerator are important
for kernel performance. To maximize performance, it is essential to overlap data
transfers with kernel execution on the FPGA. This ensures that the FPGA is
continuously processing data without waiting for transfers to complete, thereby
improving overall throughput and efficiency.
FPGAs comprise various resources, including programmable logic blocks, DSP
slices, and memory blocks. Efficient utilization of these resources is fundamental
to achieve high performance in FPGA-based accelerators.

2.2.3
HLS development for FPGAs
FPGA development using HDL allows creating highly optimized solutions for spe-
cific problems. However, design and verification times are lengthy, and the process
requires significant expertise in the underlying hardware. The use of HLS lan-
guages brings FPGA design to software development times, and it is approachable
by non-hardware experts [44]. However, to create a truly optimized HLS code for
a specific platform, certain knowledge of the underlying hardware is still required.
The verification of the design is also simplified as the tools allow to co-simulate the
software and the generated Register Transfer Level (RTL) model. RTL is a design
abstraction that represents the behavior of a synchronous digital circuit by de-
scribing how signals travel between registers and the logical operations performed
on these signals.
An interesting advantage of using HLS is that it allows to rapidly explore many
different solutions (i.e. design space exploration), which is sometimes a faster path
to converge to an optimal solution in complex problems. An equivalent exploration
using HDL would take an excessive amount of time.
High-Level Synthesis adds another level of abstraction to the hardware design
process, allowing designers to focus on larger architectural aspects and the overall
functionality of the code rather than on register-level transfers and clock-specific
operations. By hiding platform-specific implementation details such as bus proto-
cols, memory controllers, and floating-point units, HLS increases the portability
of the code across different platforms.
HLS transforms untimed high-level specifications into fully timed implemen-
tations by creating custom architectures to meet specific requirements.
These
architectures include data paths, control logic, and memory interfaces, defining
how the RTL communicates externally. The data path comprises storage elements
like registers and memories, functional units such as ALUs and multipliers, and
interconnect elements like multiplexers and buses. These components may take
multiple clock cycles to execute and can be pipelined. The process begins with
specifying an algorithm in a high-level language (e.g., C++) using specific rules
and conventions unique to HLS. It then proceeds through the following steps:
1. Compilation: following standard code optimizations.
2. Scheduling: this step involves assigning operations to specific clock cycles
based on inter-dependencies, operations latency, clock frequency, and re-
source availability.

2.2.3.1
Pipelining
Pipelining is an essential technique in hardware design that increases the frequency
of operation by adding registers to divide sequential logic paths into multiple
stages. Traditional CPU execution times are heavily affected by instruction fetch-
ing, decoding, and data movement between memory or caches. In contrast, FPGAs
allow us to create highly efficient custom architectures where data flows directly
from one computational unit to the next, minimizing unnecessary data movement
and control logic. Pipelines are essential in this design paradigm because they
allow us to maximize throughput.
Figure 2.2 shows the main attributes of pipelines, these are:
• Latency (or pipeline depth): The number of clock cycles it takes for an input
to propagate through the entire pipeline to the output.
• Initiation Interval (II): The number of clock cycles that must elapse before
the next set of inputs can be inserted into the pipeline. Ideally, we want
pipelines with an II of 1 to maximize performance.
Many algorithms in scientific computing involve repeating operations over large
data structures. Loops are a primary target for performance optimization due to
their iterative nature, which makes them time-consuming, but also exploitable for
parallelism. Using a pipeline directive on a loop or a function allows concurrent
execution of operations for each iteration of the loop or call to the function. In
other words, subsequent iterations can start without waiting for the previous ones
to finish.

into individual elements, which are then implemented using registers.

2.2.3.5
OpenCL
This open-source, cross-platform, parallel programming standard is based on a
platform-independent API that abstracts the underlying hardware.
It consists
of a host code running on a CPU that offloads computing-intensive tasks to an
heterogeneous device, hiding from the programmer the complexity of controlling
and communicating with the accelerator. The device code is written in a C-like
language, and it is called kernel code.
The OpenCL model defines a single thread as a work-item, and gathers them
into workgroups. Parallelism can be achieved at the thread level and also between
workgroups. Every work-item has its private memory and shares local memory
with all threads within a workgroup. However, the only memory shared between
workgroups is the global memory, which is usually off-chip, slow, and abundant

(in the order of GB) compared to the on-chip, fast, and scarce local memory (of
up to a few MB). OpenCL refers to the number of threads per workgroup as local
work size, and calls global work size the total number of work-items required to
solve a task (execute a kernel to completion). The standard organizes the work-
items in a workgroup in up to three dimensions. A multidimensional index then
identifies each work-item according to the number of dimensions used. This is
called NDRange model.
The Intel FPGA SDK for OpenCL allows the user to interface with the FPGA
accelerator using the device-agnostic OpenCL programming model.
This hides
the complexity of interfacing and exchanging data between FPGA and host CPU,
which is not a trivial task to do in traditional HDL-based design. It considerably
accelerates the development time at the cost of some performance degradation.
The NDRange programming model for FPGAs does not provide thread-level
parallelism by default. Instead, it creates a deep pipeline that processes all work-
items one after the other. Thread-level parallelism can be achieved through kernel
vectorization, which increases the data pipeline’s width processed by work-items
in a Single Instruction Multiple Data (SIMD) fashion. Also, the pipeline can be
replicated using Compute Unit Replication, which has the same effect of adding
thread-level parallelism, but it is usually more resource-demanding. In addition
to NDRange, Intel suggests a different model called Single Work-Item (SWI).
Instead of using of work-groups and work-items, the model structures the kernel
to be executed as a single thread where every loop is pipelined. It is the equivalent
of launching a kernel with NDRange dimensions (1,1,1). This model adapts better
to the FPGA architecture in most cases. Additional FPGA-specific optimizations,
such as loop unrolling and pipelining, can be achieved by incorporating attributes
into the kernel code.
Both Intel and AMD have supported OpenCL kernel programming from the be-
ginning, while AMD consistently favored standard C++ with pragmas as the pre-
ferred method for kernel development. In contrast, Intel initially adopted OpenCL
as the standard and later transitioned to the OneAPI DPC++ (Data Parallel
C++) compiler, aiming to unify all architectures under a single programming lan-
guage. The OneAPI Toolkit for FPGAs enables the generation of hardware models
directly from SYCL [45], a modern C++ language extension.

2.3
Performance evaluation
In this section, we review topics related to the performance evaluation of compu-
tational kernels. Specifically, we discuss the most relevant aspects of execution
time evaluation, the key metrics for power and energy consumption, and provide
a detailed description of the roofline model.
2.3.1
Basic concepts on runtime
In hardware acceleration, improving runtime is often the primary performance
objective. To ensure accurate measurements, it is recommended to execute the
kernel multiple times and average the results. There are two approaches to achieve
this:
1. Launching multiple kernel executions from the host. This approach is sim-
pler and does not require modification to the kernel. However, it is impacted
by software overhead associated with scheduling kernel executions.
2. Integrating a sequential loop into the kernel code. This method reduces the
overhead by incorporating a loop directly into the top level function of the
kernel.
Another important aspect when evaluating kernel performance is memory
transfers between the host and the accelerator, typically involving sending the
input data and retrieving the results.
These transfers are relevant due to the
lower speeds of CPU-accelerator interfaces, such as PCIe, compared to the higher
bandwidth memories in the accelerator, especially in memory-bound algorithms.
However, these transfers can often be executed in parallel with the kernel, generally
causing their timing to be concealed within the execution of the kernel.
Execution time alone may not always be the most practical performance met-
ric. The measured time often varies with the problem size, making it challenging
to compare results across different input datasets. To gain a clearer understanding
of an algorithm’s or platform’s performance, it is advantageous to use metrics that

indicates performance for integer data types, while FLOPS measures the number

When comparing performance, other valuable metrics that offer insights into

Motivated by the limited adoption of FPGAs in HPC applications — due to the

portable and open-source HLS implementation of BLAS designed for Intel FPGAs.
The library provides two levels of functionality. The first consists of OpenCL ker-
nels that implement highly parallel BLAS routines. The second offers a high-level
host API providing a C++ interface to call routines directly from the host, fol-
lowing standard BLAS calls.

The techniques employed include iteration

and tiling. The authors compare the results of their FPGA implementation against

Tan et al. (2018) [52] assess the performance of a single and double-precision
matrix-matrix multiplication OpenCL kernel on a Stratix V FPGA (DE5-NET
board).
They compare the results with an Intel i7-6800K CPU executing two
implementations: MKL and OpenBLAS. The OpenCL kernel utilizes a blocked
matrix multiplication approach, where two blocks of matrices A and B are loaded
into the internal memory of the FPGA simultaneously. The block of matrix B un-
dergoes transposition to ensure consecutive data access during computation. The
product of the two blocks is computed by a two-dimensional PE matrix, defined
by the N-dimensional space (NDRange) in the OpenCL execution model. Similar
to the classic matrix-multiplication algorithm, the inner loop is fully unrolled to
enhance parallelism for each PE. Kernel vectorization (SIMD) is applied to in-
troduce an additional level of parallelism. The authors investigate the impact on
throughput and power consumption by modifying the block size and vectorization
factor. The best-performing kernel, although notably slower than the CPU imple-
mentations, achieves improvements of 1.17× to 8.47× against MKL and 1.54× to
11.27× against OpenBLAS in terms of energy efficiency.
One of the most compelling features of OpenCL is its platform-independent na-
ture, allowing the expression of parallelism regardless of the underlying hardware.
On this grounds, Minhas et al. (2018) [53] raise the question of the performance po-
tential that an OpenCL application can attain on diverse platforms. Furthermore,
they investigate the efficiency of vendor-specific compilers in mapping OpenCL
source code to the target device with minimal or no platform-specific optimiza-
tions. They assess SGEMM and other applications on three distinct platforms:
Intel Nallatech 385 FPGA, NVIDIA GTX 980 GPU, and ARM Mali GPU. The au-
thors begin by establishing a baseline OpenCL kernel for each application through
a direct port of C code. Subsequently, they apply various platform-independent
optimizations (as part of design space exploration) to each application and evalu-
ate performance. The authors conclude that GPUs outperform FPGAs in terms of
runtime; however, FPGAs exhibit superior performance portability in the percent-
age of peak performance achieved (68% for FPGAs compared to 20% on GPUs)
and enhanced energy efficiency (up to 1.4× better for FPGAs).

computing. Matrices in Compressed Sparse Row (CSR) format with no specific
sparsity pattern are addressed. The SDE implementation comprises three stages
interconnected by mapping layers. The three stages are responsible for reading,
computing, and writing results to memory.
The mapping layers reformat the
data and distribute it using HLS Streams. This allows to read multiple coalesced
elements from memory using a wide port, enhancing the I/O bandwidth. They op-
timize the SpMV operation by transferring the entire vector x to on-chip memory,
solving non-contiguous access issues. The initial implementation is fully pipelined
and is based on the naive SpMV algorithm for CSR format. They overcome the
variable-length inner loops in CSR format by padding the matrix and adding a
next row marker to the matrix representation. They optimize the code by adding
threads for computing different rows in parallel. To reduce the number of I/O
ports required they combine the row and column indexes per thread. Each thread
requires a dedicated x vector copy, limiting problem size. The final optimization
is to balance the load between the threads, which is achieved by finding proper
matrix partitioning. This is performed by solving a 1D chains-on-chains parti-
tioning (CCP) problem. Performance testing on Zynq Ultrascale+ MPSoC using
sparse matrices from the University of Florida Sparse Matrix Collection reveals
the FPGA implementation is 4.4× faster than the CPU. Compared to GPUs, the
FPGA outperforms by an average of 3.25× for small and medium-size matrices,
while GPUs are 1.58× faster for larger matrices. In terms of energy consumption,
the FPGA is more efficient than the CPU and GPU by an average of 8.9×.
Yixiao Du et al. (2022) [61] created HiSparse, a high-performance kernel de-
signed for HBM-equipped FPGAs.
HiSparse employs a customized format for
storing sparse matrices in HBM, enabling vectorized streaming access to each
HBM channel and concurrent access to multiple channels. This optimization fully
leverages HBM’s available bandwidth for loading sparse matrices. Additionally,
HiSparse incorporates a scalable on-chip buffer design that includes vector repli-
cation and banking, supporting a significant number of parallel processing engines
(PEs) to enhance data reuse when accessing input vectors. Notably, HiSparse can
efficiently handle matrices of arbitrary size by employing matrix partitioning along
both rows and columns. The implementation was tested on an Alveo U280 using
18 HBM channels, with results compared against MKL on a 2.8 GHz Intel Xeon
Gold 6242 CPU and CuSPARSE on a GTX 1080 Ti GPU. HiSparse demonstrated
energy efficiency improvements of 37× over MKL and 3.7× over CuSPARSE.

FPGA dynamic profiler aids in the optimization process. They explore three op-

Conclusion on related works
After conducting an exhaustive review of the state-of-the-art in NLA operations
on FPGAs using high-level synthesis, we can conclude that the amount of work
in this area is modest when compared to other accelerators. The field of HLS-
based scientific computing on FPGAs remains an area with significant growth
potential. The diversity of platforms, development tools, and testing setups makes
it challenging to compare the results across studies.
Nevertheless, we present
general findings and key conclusions, focusing on the comparison between FPGA
implementations with optimized kernel libraries for CPU (e.g., MKL) and GPU
(e.g., cuBLAS and cuSPARSE):
• Compute-bound Kernels (e.g., GEMM):
– GPUs consistently outperform FPGAs in compute-bound kernels.
– CPUs generally outperform FPGAs, although there are exceptions,
particularly in single-precision tasks [51].
– FPGAs consistently consume less power and are generally more energy-
efficient than both CPUs [51,52] and GPUs [53].
– FPGAs achieve a higher percentage of peak performance compared to
GPUs when using OpenCL implementations without vendor-specific
optimizations, indicating better performance portability [53].
• Memory-bound dense routines (e.g., GEMV):
– FPGAs exhibit 25% better performance than CPUs in both single and
double precision [51].
• Memory-bound sparse routines (e.g., SpMV):
– Edge Computing Platforms: FPGAs outperform CPUs in medium-
sized platforms. Compared to GPUs, FPGAs perform better on smaller
problem sizes but worse on larger ones. FPGAs are on average 9× more
energy-efficient than both CPUs and GPUs [60].

3.1
The energy measurements laboratory
To effectively characterize both platforms and algorithms, it is important to have
a well-equipped energy laboratory and follow a specific methodology. This sec-
tion outlines the power and energy measurement setup, the devices used, and the
acceleration platforms.
Hardware accelerators need to be installed in systems alongside other com-
ponents. They are typically mounted in PCI-Express slots on CPU-based nodes.
When evaluating the energy efficiency of an algorithm running on an accelerator
compared to its CPU-only version, this dependency must be considered. However,
in many cases, it is more practical to evaluate the power consumption of accelera-
tors individually, such as when comparing similar platforms or different algorithms
on the same platform. In our laboratory, we have the capability to measure both
complete systems and individual components.
A crucial factor in leveraging different accelerators is the power consumption
in the idle state (passive power) and the percentage of time spent in this state.
High-end devices tend to consume a considerable amount of power even when idle,
and as they cannot be easily switched off, the accelerator’s usage percentage must
be high compared to the server’s total uptime. Failure to achieve this can result
in the accumulation of idle power over time, negatively impacting overall energy
efficiency. For example, the Alveo U50 accelerator card from AMD adds about
12 W of power simply by being plugged into the PCI-Express port of the server.

3.2.1.1

For the DE10-nano, we developed a simple GEMM kernel adhering to the NDRange
OpenCL paradigm, which we named GEMMEMB. This kernel is based on the tiled
matrix-multiplication algorithm, wherein the input matrices (A and B) are subdi-
vided into blocks. These blocks are then multiplied, generating partial results that
accumulate until completing the corresponding block of the solution matrix (C).
This computational method enhances data locality, optimizing memory accesses
and making use of the fast on-chip memory.
The implementation follows the OpenCL 2-dimensional NDRange model. Each
work-item within a workgroup loads an element of matrices A and B into local
memory. When blocks of size Nb × Nb are complete (synchronized using barriers),
the block-wise product is executed, and the partial results are accumulated. After
the blocks are entirely consumed, subsequent blocks are loaded and consumed until
the calculation of a block of the matrix C is completed. Each work-item within the
work-group is responsible for computing an element of the matrix C. This means
the global work size is the same as the elements in C. Refer to the pseudocode in

Sparse kernels
3.2.2.1
Kernels design
The SpMV kernel for the Intel FPGA (DE10-nano board) is based on the Spector
OpenCL benchmark suite [83], which provides a mechanism to perform a design
space exploration of the different optimization parameters. The kernel uses the
1-dimensional NDRange model. It processes one row per work-item, following the
row-based strategy used in the massively parallel context (as the scalar version
in [84]), allowing the computation of multiple rows in parallel (controlled by the
workgroup size parameter). More parallelism is added by unrolling the loops that
read the data from global into local memory and adding vectorization. Finally, it
is possible to replicate the pipeline using Compute Unit replication.
We compiled kernels with different parameters and tested their performance
on all the matrices, selecting the kernel that yielded the best execution time.
For the Alveo U50 accelerator card we developed our version of SpMV based
on the work in [60]. The kernel follows a streaming dataflow architecture, where
input data is streamed through a deep pipeline at every clock cycle. The kernel was
implemented in such a way that different tasks are compartmentalized into different
functions or blocks. These blocks then exchange data through FIFO memories
(referred to as Streams in AMD HLS). All these functions are then instantiated
with the dataflow pragma to allow concurrent execution. One block for each input
port gets the data from global memory and places it in its corresponding Stream.
The computation block reads data from the Streams, performs the product and
accumulation, and writes the results into another Stream.
Finally, the output
function is in charge of writing the results in global memory. Figure 3.3 shows a
block diagram of the implemented kernel.

performance, in each iteration L elements are processed in parallel using loop

Detailed evaluation of NLA kernels on FPGAs
In order to advance in the study of the potential of FPGAs to address NLA oper-
ations, in this section we explore and evaluate the available options for two of the
most representative kernels of BLAS, i.e. GEMV and GEMM, and fundamental
operation from sparse NLA, i.e. SpMV. All the evaluated kernels are open-source
and were developed in HLS C++ specifically for AMD devices. The evaluated
kernels are part of Vitis BLAS and Vitis sparse libraries, gemm hls from [54] and

HiSparse from [61].
AMD’s Vitis software includes a variety of performance-optimized open source
libraries designed for applications in areas such as mathematics, linear algebra,
and computer vision. The Vitis BLAS Library offers an FPGA implementation of
the Basic Linear Algebra Subprograms, which can provide significant performance
benefits for applications that require intensive linear algebra operations. This li-
brary is structured into three levels: primitives (L1), kernels (L2), and software
APIs (L3). L1 consist of parametrized C++ implementations of core BLAS opera-
tions, which can be compiled with HLS. These primitives incorporate modules for
computation and data movement, allowing developers to build high-performance
logic by interconnecting these modules. L2 provides examples of kernel implemen-
tations for host code developers, illustrating the use of L1 primitives. L3 offers
C/C++ and Python APIs to accelerate BLAS operations by utilizing pre-built
FPGA bitstreams.
The Vitis sparse library offers a high-performance HLS implementation of ba-
sic linear algebra subroutines for managing sparse matrices on FPGAs. It features
two types of implementations: primitives (L1) and kernels (L2). L1 primitives are
designed for FPGA developers, allowing them to create custom hardware designs,
while L2 kernels provide examples for system and host code developers, demon-
strating how to utilize the primitives effectively within a complete application.
For the experimental evaluation of dense and sparse kernels we used the fol-
lowing hardware: Alveo U50, Alveo U280, and Intel Xeon Silver 4208 multi-core
CPU. To compile the FPGA designs we used AMD Vitis 2022.2. For the CPU we
used MKL library.
3.3.1
Dense kernels in Vitis libraries
We evaluated the BLAS kernels from L2, which are divided in two groups. The
kernels of the first one have the same top function, which has only two ports
for communication with external memory (DRAM or HBM), and consist of an
instruction processing block, a computation unit (e.g. GEMM), and a timer unit.
The second group makes efficient use of the multichannel HBM memory to improve
communication bandwidth.
3.3.1.1
GEMM basic
The architecture of this kernel from the first group is composed of the following
blocks:
• Systolic array: Implemented using L1 primitives. Its size depends on the
datatype and the memory interface. For single precision floating point and
512 bits interface it corresponds to 16 × 16.
• Data movers: These blocks get data from global memory and send it to the
computation blocks, and vice versa.

• Transpose modules: One of the matrices must be transposed before entering
the systolic array. This block also acts as a buffer to reuse data.
3.3.1.2
GEMM Multiple Compute Units (MCU)
This kernel is implemented as two parallel instances (compute units) of the previ-
ous kernel. Each compute unit has its own dedicated HBM channel. The provided
version of this kernel uses four compute units and its intended for the Alveo U250
board. In order to fit the design in the Alveo U50 board only 2 instances could be
used. Also the DDR memory had to be changed for HBM.
3.3.1.3
GEMV basic
This kernel follows the same structure as GEMM basic, but with a custom pro-
cessing block to perform GEMV operation.
3.3.1.4
GEMV streaming
This kernel is from the second group. To maximize throughput, it instantiates N
parallel GEMV compute blocks primitives and connects each one to an individual
HBM channel via data mover modules. N can be any number from 1 to 32, which
is the maximum number of HBM channels in both Alveo boards. We evaluated
this kernel with N = 16 for the Alveo U50 and with N = 32 for the Alveo U280.

3.4.2
First evaluation of NLA kernels on FPGAs
We have explored using traditional multi-core hardware and FPGAs to address
Numerical Linear Algebra (NLA) kernels. Specifically, we studied the behavior
of highly tuned kernels in a multi-core CPU processor and HLS implementations
over FPGAs, analyzing the execution time and the energy consumption. For this
purpose, we employed the most critical kernels from dense and sparse NLA fields,
i.e., the GEMM and SpMV operations. Our work includes a brief introduction

and a revision of related work

outperforms the FPGA variants in runtime, showing a higher energy efficiency than
the small FPGA as well. However, in the sparse case, the differences in runtime
are more modest, and the performance in terms of energy consumption depends
on the matrix characteristics. Specifically, for matrices with many non-zeros, the

As stated previously, the SpMV operation is an essential kernel in the sparse
NLA field. Its performance is highly dependent on the distribution of non-zero
elements within the matrix, which influences memory access patterns and can
vary significantly across different applications.
This chapter compiles our efforts to thoroughly analyze different strategies for
optimizing the SpMV operation on FPGAs using HLS. First, we present a blocked
SpMV implementation. Next, we propose an extension of the roofline model to
incorporate energy-efficiency into the kernel optimization, and we apply it to our
blocked SpMV implementation. Following this, we offer a detailed evaluation of
the SpMV implementation from the Vitis libraries and explore various strategies
for performance optimization. One key improvement involves reducing padding by
halving the number of matrix coefficients grouped together during preprocessing,
then combining two blocks for parallel processing in the kernel.
Implementing
this approach required significant modifications to the kernel design. Finally, we
introduce a kernel designed to efficiently solve SpMV for diagonal matrices.

mulation of the partial results (Line 4 in Algorithm 1) presents a data dependency
between loop iterations. This dependency prevents the operation from producing
one result per clock cycle (i.e., pipeline parallelism). A method to hide this data
dependency is to interleave the processing of L rows simultaneously, where L is
the latency of the floating-point addition.
For this strategy to be efficient, data must be interleaved before they are read
by the FPGA, allowing contiguous memory access. To facilitate this, we opted
for the sliced ELL format, which packs the non-zero elements (and their indices),
creating dense blocks. We divide the matrix into partitions of L rows and then
apply ELL to each partition. The longest row determines the width of each block,
padding the rest of the rows with zeros to match its length. Then, the blocks are
stored in memory so that the L rows are interleaved (blocks are transposed). We
refer to the implemented kernel architecture that uses this format as Scalar.
The issue with this format is that when trying to vectorize the kernel, non-
contiguous elements of the vector x are simultaneously accessed. The previous
format is extended to address this problem so that the blocks have a fixed width
P (with ideas similar to the SELL-P sparse storage format [86]). This way, the
elements of x for each block do not have a distance greater than P. Then, we can
partition the x cache in the FPGA to allow P simultaneous accesses. We show an
example of the sparse format in Figure 4.1. In addition to the data and column
indices, the format requires a vector indicating the number of dense blocks per row

4.2
Optimizing SpMV guided by the Roofline Model
Besides the empirical studies, it is also interesting to apply analytical tools to
understand our developments’ performance and guide the kernels’ optimization
process. Several research works focus on developing models and frameworks to
estimate the performance of FPGA designs [87–89]. In this sense, the roofline
model (RLM) [50] is a graphical tool that can help analyze the computational
performance and the main bottlenecks of a specified software when it runs in
a particular hardware platform. Specifically, the RLM is a chart that relates the
computational performance (usually measured in floating-point operations per sec-
ond, FLOPS) with the arithmetic intensity (the ratio of floating-point operations
per byte of memory transferred). The chart also shows the memory bandwidth
and arithmetic performance bounds of the hardware. The RLM is explained in
more detail in Section 2.3.3.
63


Chapter 4. Sparse NLA developments
This section presents our efforts in developing an extension of the RLM that
allows the optimization of performance and energy consumption of NLA kernels
based on sparse block format storage on FPGAs. The model works on operations
per number of memory accesses instead of the traditional computational intensity
(in operations per bytes transferred). Additionally, it features a quick mechanism
to find the performance and energy efficiency of sparse algebra kernels that use
sparse block representation formats. To put our RLM model to test, we apply it
to the Scalar kernel and its improved version, Block, that exploits a block-sparse
storage format to enable more efficient data access.
4.2.1
The RLM as a Guide to Optimizing the Performance of
Blockwise SpMV
The reviewed works in Section 2.4.3 provide detailed information about employing
the RLM in optimizing the SpMV for implementations where the operation count
and data transfers can be directly derived from the number of non-zeros of the
sparse matrix. However, these models are inaccurate for sparse formats such as
ELLPACK, where a certain amount of padding is allowed to improve memory
performance. Therefore, we propose an adaptation of the RLM that considers the
padding to study the bottlenecks in our sparse matrix kernels. In other words, we
offer a methodology to leverage the RLM to optimize block-sparse codes in FPGAs,
where the key is the procedure to increase the computational intensity when the
kernel is in the memory-bound region (blue zone in Figure 2.5). The advantage of
the RLM is that it provides straightforward visual verification of the procedure.
Some related ideas were previously presented for dense algebra methods running
in GPUs [90].
We define the model’s vertical axis as performance in GFLOPS and the horizon-
tal axis as CIA (Computational Intensity per Access), representing floating-point
operations per memory access. For sparse blocked formats, this metric is related
to the density of the blocks. With this definition of CIA, the bandwidth roof is
expressed in giga memory accesses per second. Consequently, an increase in the
operation count due to a rising amount of data transferred in each memory access
impacts the intensity but not the bandwidth.
Sparse codes that employ zero-padded blocks reach two different intensities:
the theoretical intensity, defined by the block’s dimension, and the useful intensity,
which only considers the number of non-zero coefficients in each block. We employ
the second one, computed using the average of non-zero coefficients per block,
since counting floating-point operations performed with zeros artificially increases
computational intensity and performance.
Therefore, the CIA reached by the
SpMV in our model depends on the block dimension and the sparse matrix pattern.
In summary, a kernel’s position within our RLM extension depends not only on
the computing hardware platform (the FPGA) and the (block) computer solver,
as is typically the case in RLM, but also on the non-zero coefficient pattern of the
matrix.

4.3
Evaluation of SpMV from Vitis Libraries
The main motivations behind benchmarking HLS SpMV kernels in FPGAs are
as follows. First, it is essential to assess the performance benefits and trade-offs
of FPGA acceleration for SpMV. Second, given the rapid evolution of HLS tools
and FPGA architectures, there is a need to establish comprehensive benchmarking
frameworks that can guide researchers in optimizing FPGA-based designs. Third,
due to the great variety of sparse matrices and the wide range of strategies to
parallelize the SpMV operation in FPGAs, it is interesting to understand which
set of design techniques better suits the matrix’s characteristics.
Additionally,
it is worthwhile to analyze matrix preprocessing techniques (e.g., reordering) to
improve the efficiency of the kernel.
This section addresses these challenges by presenting a comprehensive bench-
marking study of the available state-of-the-art SpMV kernels developed using HLS.
We focus on the Alveo platforms by AMD, and in the first stage, we evaluate the
SpMV kernel from Vitis Libraries. Later, we propose different strategies to im-
prove performance, achieving considerable speedups.
4.3.1
Sparse Vitis libraries
AMD’s Vitis software includes a range of performance-optimized open-source li-
braries for various purposes, including math, linear algebra, and computer vision.
The Vitis sparse library [64] is a fast and efficient HLS implementation of the basic
linear algebra subroutines for handling sparse matrices on FPGAs.
There are currently two implementations of SpMV, both targeting AMD’s
HBM-equipped FPGAs, such as the Alveo U280. The first one (CSCMV) adopts
the Compressed Sparse Column (CSC) format and exploits parallelism at the col-
umn level. It possesses 16 independent compute pipelines, each connected to its
own HBM channel, and uses single-precision floating point. However, it has the
limitation of being unable to process large matrices.
71

The second implementation (spmv double benchmark) also comprises 16 com-
pute paths with independent memory connections but is based on the CSR format.
The input matrix undergoes preprocessing (partitioning) to evenly distribute its el-
ements along the compute paths and extract the indices and parameters needed by
the kernel. To enable continuous kernel execution without stalling, the partitions
are padded with zeros, which can potentially lead to performance degradation
depending on the kernel configuration and matrix characteristics.
This imple-
mentation employs double-precision floating-point arithmetic and accommodates
matrices of any size as long as they fit into memory.
In this work, we evaluate spmv double because it is the better performing of
the two and does not have a restriction regarding matrix size.
The SpMV accelerator architecture consists of 24 compute units (CUs) con-
nected via AXI streams, which enables the highest degree of parallelism. We show
the architecture in Figure 4.6. This design uses 16 HBM channels to store the
non-zero values and indices of a sparse matrix. Each HBM channel feeds a ded-
icated computation path to perform the SpMV operation for the portion of the
sparse matrix data stored in that channel. As a result, 16 SpMV operations are
performed simultaneously on different sections of the sparse matrix data. The host
does the partitioning of the sparse matrix data before executing the kernel, which
processes one partition at a time.
The design requires four additional HBM channels: two for storing partition
information, one for the input dense vector, and one for the result vector. The
loadParX kernel reads elements from the input vector and the partition parame-
ters, then transfers the data to the fwdParParam kernel. This kernel distributes
the partition parameters to the 16 compute cores (selMultX) and forwards the
vector to the moveX kernel, which propagates the vector elements needed by each
computing module. The vector element propagation works as follows: all elements
corresponding to the currently processed partition are read and passed through
the moveX kernel, which uses partition information to determine the necessary el-
ements for each selMultX kernel. A more detailed explanation can be found on
Appendix B.1. The loadRowParam kernel reads partition parameters required for
accumulation stages and assembling the result vector.
The loadNnz kernel reads the matrix coefficients and their indices from ex-
ternal memory and distributes them to the selMultX kernels, which perform the
dot product between arrays of coefficients and their corresponding dense vector
elements.
The width of the memory access is determined by the parEntries
parameter, set to 4 for double precision (and 8 for single precision), imposing a
memory width of 256 bits. This parameter also determines the vectorization of
the compute path, allowing each compute path to perform parEntries operations
in parallel every cycle. The selMultX kernel also performs a partial accumula-
tion of results, the amount is determined by the accLatency parameter. Since
floating-point accumulation in Alveo FPGAs requires multiple clock cycles, the
kernel loads accLatency partial results into local memory and performs the re-
duction in accLatency clock cycles. This approach ensures that the reduction core
can read one partial result each clock cycle, preventing data flow stalls through

The partially accumulated results from the selMultX kernels are sent to rowAcc,
which performs accumulation across an entire row of partitions (row of blocks).
The rowAcc kernel operates in two stages. First, it accumulates the partial results
row-wise in local memory, with each entry corresponding to an element of the re-
sult vector. The latency of this operation is defined by the accLatency parameter,
but there is no stalling issue because the previous block already reduces the speed
of generating new data by a factor of accLatency. In the second stage, the kernel
accumulates the results stored in the local memories of all channels and forwards
them, ordered in ascending row order, to the assembleY core. This kernel assem-
bles the result vector and sends it to the storeY kernel, responsible for transferring
it to external memory.
All modules without direct access to external memory are configured as free-
running, simplifying the logic and reducing overhead. Moreover, the kernels are
strategically placed within the FPGA fabric to minimize crossings between super
logic regions, thereby improving timing.

4.3.2
Description of the Sparse Matrix Format
The matrix partitioning algorithm is implemented in Python and employs a three-
tiered partitioning strategy: The first level divides the matrix along its rows into
Row Blocks (Rb). These Row Blocks contain fewer than 4K rows, a limit set by the
maxRows parameter configuration. In the second level of partitioning, each Row
Block (Rb) is further partitioned along the columns into Partitions (P). These
Partitions are structured to contain fewer than 4K columns based on the maxCols
parameter. In the third level of partitioning, each Partition (P) is evenly divided
into 16 segments, called Channel Partitions (ChP).
To optimize double precision accumulation with an 8-cycle latency, the num-
ber of non-zero Elements in each row of the Channel Partition is padded to be
a multiple of 8×parEntries. In addition, the data within each Channel Parti-
tion is organized in a row-major order to enhance memory access patterns during
computation.

4.3.3
Kernel Adaptation
As a first step, we implemented a single-precision version to align with the common
practice of reducing precision to enhance performance.
The AMD design originally uses double-precision floating-point.
To enable
single-precision operation, modifications were required in both the kernel code and
preprocessing scripts. The kernel library is parameterized using template functions
and macros, allowing for easy adjustments to parameters such as memory interface
bit width, the number of elements processed in parallel, the number of channels,
data type, and index bit width. However, the spmv double benchmark design was
specifically optimized for double precision. To achieve this, some functions were
designed to group multiple parameters interleaved with data. When reducing the
data bit width from 64 to 32, these groupings became incompatible and required
redesign. Additionally, the preprocessing scripts were not parameterizable based
on data type, so support for single precision had to be explicitly added.

4.5
Optimized Vitis kernel architecture
One of the main drawbacks of the Vitis SpMV kernel is that it often produces
a considerable amount of padding.
This is especially true for single precision,
where we increase the parEntries parameter to double the number of coeffi-
cients processed per cycle. Increasing parEntries results in excessive padding
because non-zero elements are always grouped into blocks of size parEntries,
84


4.5. Optimized Vitis kernel architecture
without grouping consecutive elements together. If coefficients are not consecu-
tive, the blocks are padded with zeros.
Additionally, the minimum number of
blocks per row is determined by the accLatency parameter, resulting in a mini-
mum of parEntries×accLatency = 64 elements per row for single precision. For
reference, the average padding ratio is 3.3 for double precision and 5.8 for single
precision.
In this section, we propose a modification to the kernel architecture to reduce
padding and thereby improve performance. The idea is to preprocess the matrix
by generating blocks of size parEntries = 4, but then read and process these in
the kernel in groups of size 8, that is, two blocks at a time. Depending on the
matrix structure, this approach could potentially cut padding in half and thus
double the performance. However, as we will see later, the theoretical limit for
padding savings is less than half, because we must also account for the indices,
which are interleaved with the data.
With this strategy, the blocks read by the kernel do not necessarily correspond
to consecutive row elements, as it groups two non-contiguous blocks of 4. This
means we need to modify the kernel design to correctly access the elements of
the dense vector for the multiplication. See Appendix B for a detailed explana-
tion on the dense vector propagation (Seccion B.1) and the modification made
(Section B.2).
We refer to the optimized kernel as floatPadd, and for comparison purposes,
we refer to the original kernel as floatOrig. In Table 4.9, we present the results for
the floatPadd version with a partition size of 4k. The number of partitions (#P)
is shown in the second column, which remains the same as in the previous version.
Columns 3 to 6 compare the runtime and padding ratio against the floatOrig
version. The eighth column shows that there is a runtime improvement in most
cases. However, the padding decrease (7th column) does not always match the
runtime improvement. Results are grouped according to the difference between
the padding decrease and the runtime decrease, which we will explore further in
the next sections.
4.5.1
Effect on padding
Row and column indices are packed and interleaved with the non-zero elements
as follows. The indices are grouped according to the amount that fits within the
memory interface width, defined by the parameter memWidth and the number of
bits used to represent the indices. memWidth depends on the data type and the
parameter parEntries. For example, in single precision (32bits) with parEntries
set to 8, a coefficient packet occupies 256 bits, which sets memWidth to 256. Regard-
ing the indices bitwidth, since the design uses relative indices, their value remains
small regardless of the matrix size, allowing them to be represented with 16 bits.
As a consequence, indices are packed in groups of 256/16 = 16. This means a
packet of column indices is sent every 16 coefficient blocks. And, since the mini-
mum number of coefficients blocks per row is accLatency, row index packets are
sent every 16×8 coefficient blocks.

4.6
SpMV for banded matrices
The SpMV kernel from the previous section has weaker performance for matrices
with few elements per row. This is the case for diagonal or banded matrices (e.g.,
qpband). Moreover, we saw that applying the RCM algorithm, which transforms
the matrix structure to group elements near the diagonal, does not generally yield
better results for these kernels. For these reasons, we developed an SpMV kernel
optimized for banded matrices, which is the purpose of this section. The idea is
to target those matrices that performed poorly with the Vitis Libraries kernels
and also seek performance improvements in matrices transformed with the RCM
algorithm.
In a more general sense, the SpMV operation for diagonal sparse
matrices is particularly significant in computational science [84, 92, 93], e.g. the
solution of partial differential equations (PDEs).
Given the limitations of the Vitis kernel discussed in the previous section, our
proposal is to develop a SpMV kernel specifically optimized for diagonal matrices.
This kernel can be applied to purely diagonal matrices or used as part of a hybrid
scheme. In this scheme, the diagonals of the matrix are extracted and processed
with our kernel, while the remaining elements are handled using another method.
In section 4.6.3 we include a study to determine which cases could be benefit from
a hybrid scheme.
The following sections presents our proposed solution. First, we describe the
representation format used and some preprocessing considerations. Then, we out-
line the implemented kernel architecture.
4.6.1
Representation format
When the non-zero elements of a sparse matrix are organized along specific diag-
onals, it is possible to store only these elements and their relative positions to the
main diagonal. This is the principle of the Diagonal (DIA) representation format.
The strategy for solving SpMV using this format leverages the regular structure
of the matrix.
The representation format we used is based on the DIA format, but we added a
partitioning scheme to optimize the kernel operation that computes SpMV block-
wise for banded matrices. Figure 4.11 shows a graphic representation of the utilized
format. Diagonals of the matrix are not required to be contiguous.
The preprocessing stage is as follows: First, diagonals of the matrix are stored
as columns of a new matrix with dimensions rows×bandwidth1. Sub-diagonals
are padded to equal the matrix row size. Specifically, diagonals below the main
diagonal are padded with leading zeros, while diagonals above the main diagonal
are padded with trailing zeros. Then, the rows of the new matrix are padded to
be a multiple of the block size (maxRows). Subsequently, the columns are padded
to be a multiple of the kernel’s datapath (parEntries). For each block, rows are
grouped according to the number of compute channels used in the kernel, which

4.6.2
Implemented kernel
We developed a kernel that leverages HBM’s bandwidth to efficiently compute
parallel SpMV. The implementation was done using the AMD HLS C++ and
compiled with Vitis Software version 2022.2 for the Alveo U280 accelerator card.
The kernel is configured to use single precision for all operations.
The kernel architecture is shown in Figure 4.12. It consists of multiple compute
units connected via streams. There are 16 compute channels that work on different
rows in parallel. The compute channels are divided into two groups of 8, with each
group processing half of the matrix. Each compute channel has exclusive access to
external memory (HBM) to read the matrix coefficients. Additionally, each group
of compute channels has a dedicated block to read the corresponding elements of
the vector x.

For a banded matrix, the elements of the dense vector needed to compute the
dot product with a given row of the band can be obtained by sliding the window
of elements corresponding to the previous row one position to the right along the
dense vector. This ensures spatial locality in accessing both the coefficients and
the vector elements. For each block of rows, the kernel reads from memory packets
of consecutive dense vector elements of size parEntries. Each packet is streamed
through the compute channels in a systolic array fashion, and then each channel
shifts the packets according to the position of the rows it is processing.
The
regular structure of the matrix data and chosen kernel parameters (numChannels
and parEntries) ensures that each channel always shifts the same number of
positions.
The compute blocks receive a packet of coefficients and the corresponding
elements of vector x and perform the dot product between them.
The loop is
structured in a pipeline such that a partial result is generated every clock cycle.
The partial results are sent to the accumulation blocks.
The accumulation blocks have local memory where they accumulate the par-
tial results of each row. Each compute block has its own accumulation block for
the partial results of specific rows within each block of rows. The matrix repre-
sentation and partitioning scheme are crucial in the accumulation process. Due
to the high latency (L) of floating-point addition operations on the FPGAs used,
it is not possible to generate a pipeline that accepts new data to accumulate in
each iteration, as dependencies are created between iterations. That is, iteration
n + 1 must wait for the result of iteration n to complete. This can be resolved by
interleaving the accumulation of M rows, provided that M is greater than L.
After accumulation, it is necessary to empty the local memory and send the
results to the block that gathers the results from all channels (and subsequently
writes them to external memory). The emptying process takes time, as the mem-
ory is read at a rate of one packet per cycle (taking maxRows ÷ numChannels ÷
parEntries cycles). To avoid stalling the kernel execution while waiting for the
memory to empty, two reduction blocks are instantiated in parallel for each chan-
nel, and their execution is interleaved between blocks of rows. Thus, when one is
sending out the results, the other can continue processing the next block.

Chapter conclusions
4.7.1
Optimizing SpMV guided by the Roofline Model
We have proposed an extension of the roofline model for FPGAs intended to
optimize sparse linear algebra kernels based on blocked representation formats,
both from the runtime and energy consumption perspectives. In particular, we
implemented a SpMV kernel that leverages a block-sparse storage format to attain
concurrency in the data access and parallelism in the computations.
The experimental evaluation of our methods, performed on a cutting-edge
FPGA, confirms the benefits of this kind of block format for sparse algebra. In
the same line, the proposed use of the RLM allows the selection of the best op-
tion (between the Scalar algorithm and the Block algorithm with different block
dimensions) to improve the runtime and energy consumption effortlessly.

4.7. Chapter conclusions
4.7.2
Evaluation and tuning of SpMV from Vitis libraries
We evaluated the HLS implementation of the SpMV from the Vitis libraries in the
AMD Alveo U280 FPGA. In the initial phase of our study, we assessed the perfor-
mance of the original kernel (in double precision) and our modified version in single
precision. We observed a linear relationship between runtime and nnz. Further-
more, we noted that due to excessive padding, transitioning to single precision and
increasing parallelism only sometimes yields a corresponding performance boost.
Another finding is that matrices with very few partitions exhibit a performance
degradation.
In the second phase, we proposed techniques to improve performance and eval-
uated its impact on the tested matrices. Specifically, we modified the partition size
and found that in cases with matrices containing fewer nnz, it is advantageous to
use smaller partition dimensions. Subsequently, we examined the effect of applying
RCM reordering to the input matrix. Except for some cases that achieve improve-
ments between 40% and 60%, applying RCM resulted in moderate or negligible
enhancements. This can be attributed to the fact that it did not significantly re-
duce the padding. Finally, we explored a hybrid format in which a percentage of
the non-zero elements in the matrix is removed, aiming to achieve even more sub-
stantial padding reduction and a decrease in the number of partitions, ultimately
improving the execution time.
By selecting the best results from all experiments for each matrix, we achieved
an average improvement in execution time of 1.4×, and up to 3.2× in the best-case
scenario for the second stage.
4.7.3
Optimization of SpMV from Vitis libraries
Building on the previous stdy, in the final stage, we introduced modifications to
the kernel design aimed at reducing padding. Specifically, the preprocessing step
reduces the block size by half while maintaining the kernel datapath width un-
changed. This adjustment requires modifications to the kernel design, as the blocks
processed in the kernel now consist of two smaller, potentially non-consecutive
blocks. This change has significant implications for handling the selection of dense
vector elements to multiply with the matrix coefficients. The idea behind halving
the block size was to reduce padding by half. However, due to the interleaving
of indices between the coefficients, the actual reduction was less than expected.
Despite this, we achieved noteworthy runtime reductions.
By selecting the best results from all experiments for each matrix, we achieved
an average improvement in execution time of 1.5×, with up to 3.7× in the best
case compared against the original kernel from Vitis libraries.
4.7.4
SpMV for banded matrices
We presented the development of an SpMV kernel for diagonal matrices, imple-
mented using HLS for FPGAs and single-precision computations. Our implemen-
tation processes band matrices with any number of diagonals, which do not need
