computation channels that process 16 rows in parallel. Each computation channel
has access to an independent HBM channel.
To evaluate its performance, we utilized a set of sparse matrices with different
characteristics and extracted a bandwidth (of size 8 and 24) to which we applied
the kernel. The execution time results were promising. Additionally, we evaluated
the Vitis library’s SpMV kernel on the same matrices and compared the results
to assess the potential benefits of a hybrid scheme, where our kernel handles the
diagonal bandwidth, and another method handles the remaining elements.
We defined two metrics for the comparison: the difference in nnz processed by
each kernel and the difference in execution time. If the execution time benefits
outweigh the reduction in nnz, a hybrid scheme would likely be advantageous.
We repeated all experiments after applying the RCM ordering to the matrices.
The results indicated that in 25 to 26 out of 33 cases, a hybrid scheme would be
beneficial.

5.1
Concluding remarks
Since the end of Dennard scaling, power consumption has become one of the pri-
mary constraints in hardware design because it no longer scales proportionally with
transistor size. With this restriction, the field of high-performance computing faces
the challenge of meeting the growing demand for computational capacity. In this
context, heterogeneous devices, such as FPGAs, play a crucial role in providing
the required computational power while maintaining energy efficiency. FPGAs are
massively parallel and highly energy-efficient devices, but their design process is
complex and requires specialized expertise. However, this could change with the
introduction of HLS tools. In this thesis, we aimed to explore the use of FPGAs
and HLS tools to develop numerical linear algebra kernels, focusing on improving
performance and energy efficiency.
In Chapter 3, we detailed the development of a laboratory capable of measuring
the power consumption of heterogeneous platforms or complete systems, integrated
with pmlib software to automate these measurements. This setup includes var-
ious FPGA platforms, the server housing them, and the necessary development
tools, all accessible remotely. This constitutes a very important step, not only
for this thesis but also for establishing a new research line at our school focused
on hardware acceleration in FPGAs for high-performance computing. We then
presented our initial results exploring FPGAs and traditional multi-core CPUs
for addressing NLA kernels such as GEMM, GEMV, and SpMV. We evaluated
both performance and energy consumption. Our findings indicate that for dense
problems, CPUs outperform FPGA variants. However, in the sparse case, the dif-
ferences in runtime are more modest, and energy consumption performance varies
depending on matrix characteristics.
In Chapter 4, we explored various strategies for optimizing the SpMV oper-
ation on FPGAs using HLS. First, we presented a novel extension of the roofline
model for FPGAs aimed at optimizing the performance and energy efficiency of
SpMV kernels based on blocked representation formats. Our SpMV implemen-
tation using this format was evaluated on Alveo accelerator cards, demonstrating


Chapter 5. Conclusion and future work
the benefits of the block format for sparse algebra. The proposed extension of the
RLM enables the selection of the best option between two SpMV implementa-
tions with different block dimensions, improving runtime and energy consumption
effortlessly.
Second, we evaluated the HLS implementation of SpMV from the Vitis li-
braries on the Alveo U280 FPGA. Initially, we assessed performance for different
parameters and data types, analyzing the effects of padding and matrix partition-
ing. In the subsequent phase, we proposed techniques to enhance performance,
specifically modifying the partition size. We found that for matrices with fewer
non-zero elements (nnz), smaller partition dimensions were advantageous. We also
examined the impact of applying RCM reordering to the input matrix, resulting
in moderate or negligible improvements. Furthermore, we explored a hybrid for-
mat to achieve substantial padding reduction and fewer partitions, significantly
improving execution time.
Finally, we propose a kernel modification to reduce padding by halving the
number of matrix coefficients grouped together during preprocessing, followed by
combining two blocks for parallel processing within the kernel. Implementing this
approach required significant changes to the kernel design, particularly addressing
the dispatch of vector x elements, which became non-contiguous after the modifi-
cation. While the reduction in padding was noticeable, it was somewhat limited
due to the overhead of the row and column indices interleaved with the matrix
coefficients. Additionally, for some matrices, performance improvements were lim-
ited by the kernel’s inefficiency in handling matrices with a low number of non-zero
elements per row.
By integrating all the proposed optimization techniques, we achieved substan-
tial performance improvements for most matrices tested with the Vitis SpMV ker-
nel, which is recognized as the state-of-the-art HLS implementation for FPGAs.
Overall, our approach resulted in an average speedup of 1.5×, with a maximum
speedup of 3.7×.
Lastly, we developed an SpMV kernel optimized for diagonal matrices, showing
promising performance results. Additionally, we evaluated the benefits of a hybrid
scheme where our kernel handles the diagonal part of a matrix, and another method
handles the remaining elements. Our analysis indicated that in 25 to 26 out of 33
cases, a hybrid scheme would be beneficial.
In conclusion, this thesis presents a comprehensive experimental evaluation of
both existing open-source libraries and our own implementations of fundamental
numerical linear algebra kernels on FPGAs using HLS. Our findings indicate that
for dense linear algebra operations, FPGAs are generally less competitive in perfor-
mance compared to multicore processors. However, significant potential exists to
enhance performance and particularly energy efficiency in applications constrained
by memory bandwidth, such as SpMV.
The adoption of HLS tools shows promise in bridging the gap between FPGA
hardware design and high-performance computing software development, simplify-
ing complex tasks like system integration, simulation, and design space exploration.
Nevertheless, optimizing kernels on FPGAs with HLS still requires a certain level

5.3
Future work
A guiding principle for this thesis is to understand not only what makes an al-
gorithm more efficient but also which hardware platforms are best for certain
workloads.
To achieve this, it is imperative to experiment with multiple plat-
forms. We focused our work on AMD accelerator cards because, at the time of
acquiring the devices, we had a limited budget. Additionally, we evaluated that
both the platforms and the HLS tools from AMD appeared more mature and had
a larger user base in academic works. In the near future, we aim to expand our
experiments to include Intel platforms. We have recently acquired two Terasic
platforms featuring the latest generation Intel Agilex FPGA. These devices have
dedicated DSP blocks with native support for floating-point operations, and it
would be interesting to examine how this feature affects the studied NLA kernels.
It would also be interesting to evaluate the new AMD heterogeneous SoC architec-
ture, the Versal ACAP [46], built on the TSMC 7 nm FinFET process technology.
These devices integrate three different types of processing units: Adaptable En-
gines, which is the classical programmable logic of modern FPGAs; Scalar Engines,
which are integrated processor systems (PS); and AI Engines, which are an array
of specialized processing units optimized for digital signal processing and machine
learning. AI Engines utilize Single Instruction Multiple Data (SIMD) and Very
Long Instruction Word (VLIW) architectures.
In line with the above, it would also be interesting to include other heteroge-
neous platforms, such as GPU and Tensor Processing Units (TPU), in the eval-
uation to perform a more comprehensive comparison. The ultimate goal of this
multi-platform evaluation would be to develop models for the automatic prediction
of which hardware platform will offer the best performance and energy efficiency
for a given problem.
In future work, we plan to extend the evaluation to other NLA operations.
Specifically, we aim to explore the Sparse Triangular Solver (SpTRSV) kernel on
high-end FPGA platforms, as we have only evaluated an embedded FPGA for
this kernel. Additionally, we intend to test some of the optimized NLA kernels in
real-world applications to assess the practical gains of the optimized developments.
Regarding the block-wise SpMV and the roofline model extension, we intend
to extend our optimization strategies to other sparse NLA kernels, such as Sparse
Matrix to Dense Matrix Multiplication (SpMM), General Sparse Matrix-Matrix
Multiplication (SpGEMM), and SpTRSV, and evaluate the effectiveness of our
RLM extension. Additionally, we will explore sparse matrix reordering techniques
to understand the impact of computational intensity on the performance of our
kernels. Concerning the evaluation and optimization of the Vitis libraries, we aim
to investigate more methods for reducing padding. For the hybrid format, devel-
oping an automated method to identify the elements that are most beneficial to

Appendix B
Read and propagation of the dense
vector for spmv double benchmark
kernel
B.1
Original version
The following describes the data flow of the elements of dense vector (x) from
external memory to the compute blocks.
During the preprocessing stage, metadata is generated to assist the kernel op-
eration. This metadata includes the number of elements of the dense vector (numX)
required for each partition and the starting index (startAddr), which points to
the location of the numX elements within the x vector.
For each partition, the smallest and largest column indices of the coefficients
are obtained.
Then, numX is equal to the distance between these indices, and
startAddr is equal to the smallest index. The numX vector elements are consec-
utive, which is necessary for efficient access to the external memory, but not all
elements are used in the kernel. This is a potential inefficiency in the kernel design:
when a partition has very few non-zero elements that are spread far apart, time is
wasted reading x elements that are ultimately discarded.
The numX elements are loaded from external memory and sent via a stream to
the moveX kernel. The moveX kernel consists of a systolic array with 16 blocks,
where each one receives a stream of dense vector elements and forwards it to the
next. Each block has an output connected to its corresponding selMultX kernel,
to which it sends the required x elements. To determine the required x elements,
each block from the moveX kernel receives its independent start and finish index.
When the vector elements blocks are received in the selMultX kernel, they are
stored in a local memory in increasing order. The size of the memory is:
depth × width = (maxCols/parEntries) × (parEntries × dataBits)
= (4096/8) × (8 × 32b)
= 512 × 256b

where maxCols is the maximum number of columns per partition.
As the xs
blocks are read and propagated in consecutive order, there is no need for indices
to store them in order. However, when performing computations, the x elements
are accessed randomly due to the sparsity of the matrix. Each matrix coefficient is
accompanied by its corresponding column index, which is used to read the vector
element from local memory. Since these local memories are constructed with block
RAMs inside the FPGA, its random access is very fast, allowing one block to be
extracted every clock cycle.
B.2
Modifications for floatPadd
In the floatPadd version, the preprocessing stage groups elements by half the width
of the kernel’s data path, aiming to minimize the amount of padding required. This
means that the dense vector elements blocks and their corresponding metadata (see
previous section) are also generated according to this configuration. Consequently,
modifications had to be made to the kernel to adapt the indices and sizes to the
floatPadd requirements.
The major modification was made to the cache for x elements inside the
selMultX kernel.
As stated earlier, we store the blocks of x elements in con-
secutive order. The difference now is that we store or load two blocks in each
iteration. For example, in the loop that reads the values from the local memory,
first, two indices are read from an input stream, second, we perform two random
accesses to the local memory using the indices. Last, we join both blocks and
propagate them to the compute core via an output stream. All this is scheduled
in a loop with II=1. In conclusion, memories have to support two simultaneous
write operations in the loading stage and two simultaneous read operations when
retrieving the x blocks. Fortunately, the BRAM blocks in the Ultrascale architec-
ture support true dual-port RAM operation, so this optimization can be achieved
without additional resource cost.

Abstract: Since the end of Dennard scaling, power consumption has become a primary con- straint in computing hardware design because it no longer scales proportionally with transistor size. The push for increased performance has led manufacturers to develop multi-core devices, revolutionizing the field over the past few decades. Recently, the High Performance Computing field has focused on energy-efficient heterogeneous platforms, with Field-Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGAs) gaining attention due to their superior energy efficiency. Traditionally, FPGAs were ex- cluded from mainstream software development due to the complex design process, but this is changing with the introduction of High-Level Synthesis (HLS) tools that generate hardware descriptions from standard programming languages like C++. Numerical Linear Algebra (NLA) traverses several disciplines of science and engineering and is crucial in scientific computing. Solving problems in these ar- eas often involves basic NLA operations, which are typically the most computa- tionally expensive steps. This thesis focuses on developing and evaluating NLA kernels using HLS tools on modern FPGA-based platforms. To support this, we set up a laboratory for measuring the performance and energy consumption of heterogeneous platforms. This step involves the acquisition and installation of FPGA-based acceleration platforms, along with the necessary development tools and infrastructure. The thesis evaluates the performance of FPGAs for both dense and sparse NLA operations using floating-point arithmetic, comparing the results against multi-core CPUs. The study begins with a review of the state-of-the-art in HLS implementations on FPGA. It then explores developments in two of the most prominent dense linear algebra kernels: matrix-vector multiplication (GEMV) and matrix-matrix multi- plication (GEMM). Additionally, the thesis focuses on one of the key kernels in sparse linear algebra, sparse matrix-vector multiplication (SpMV). The findings indicate that while CPUs often outperform FPGAs in dense operations, FPGAs offer competitive energy efficiency. For sparse operations, FPGAs not only de- liver competitive performance but also consistently demonstrate superior energy efficiency. A key aspect of maximizing kernel efficiency is exploring analytical tools to understand performance and guide the optimization process. The roofline model (RLM) is a well-known graphical tool that facilitates the analysis of computational performance and identifies primary bottlenecks. We propose a novel extension of the RLM for FPGAs to assist in the optimization of runtime and energy con- sumption for NLA kernels based on sparse blocked storage formats. We apply this extended model to our SpMV kernel with a block-sparse storage format. The final effort in this thesis focuses on the analysis and extension of AMD’s Vitis library for the SpMV operation, recognized as state-of-the-art in the field. Several optimizations and matrix preprocessing techniques were explored, leading to significant performance gains. Among these extensions, techniques were intro- duced that combine reducing block sizes (to minimize padding) with the concurrent processing of multiple blocks (to compensate for the reduced data processed per block). For single precision, the optimizations achieved an average speedup of 1.5× and a maximum of 3.7×. Furthermore, a custom SpMV kernel optimized for band matrices was developed, delivering substantial performance improvements over the Vitis kernel for these kind of matrices. iv Contents Resumen
